title: Explain store inputs categories, labeling and storage methods

lessons.title: Categories of farm store inputs
lessons.html:
Why categorise inputs?

A farm store holds valuable and sometimes dangerous inputs. Grouping them into categories makes it easier to store them safely, find them quickly, control stock and prevent contamination.

Main categories

CategoryExamplesMain risks
AgrochemicalsHerbicides, insecticides, fungicides, rodenticidesPoisoning, fire, pollution, contamination of food and feed
FertilisersUrea, LAN, superphosphate, compound mixes, limeMoisture damage, caking; some (e.g. ammonium nitrate products) are oxidisers and fire or explosion risks
Veterinary productsVaccines, dips, dewormers, antibiotics, syringesLoss of potency if not kept at correct temperature; misuse; residues in meat and milk
Seed and propagation materialCertified seed, treated seed, bulbs, seedlingsMoisture, heat, rodents; treated seed is toxic
Animal feedPellets, licks, maize, hayMould, rodents, contamination with chemicals
Fuel and lubricantsDiesel, petrol, oil, greaseFire, spills, theft
PackagingCartons, crates, bags, labelsContamination, pests
Tools, spares and PPEFilters, belts, gloves, respiratorsLoss, theft, damage

Separation rules

  • Keep agrochemicals in their own locked store, never with feed, seed for food, or food.
  • Store fertilisers apart from fuels and chemicals; keep oxidising fertilisers away from flammable materials.
  • Keep herbicides separate from other pesticides to avoid cross-contamination.
  • Keep vaccines in a dedicated fridge, not with food.
  • Store fuel in an approved, bunded area away from buildings.

Agricultural remedies and stock remedies are regulated under the Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act 36 of 1947.

lessons.title: Labels and storage methods
lessons.html:
Reading product labels

The label is the legal instruction for using a registered product. Before storing or issuing it, check:

  • Product name, active ingredient and registration number
  • Hazard classification and warning symbols or colour band
  • Storage conditions (temperature, keep dry, keep away from sunlight)
  • First aid instructions and emergency numbers
  • Withholding or re-entry periods (always take these from the label; never guess)
  • Batch number and expiry date

Never remove labels or decant chemicals into unmarked or food and drink containers. If a label is damaged, report it so the product can be identified and relabelled correctly.

Shelf and bin labels

Label shelves and bins with the product name and category. Use a clear layout so the same product is always in the same place.

Storage methods

  • Chemical store: locked, ventilated, fire-resistant, with a bunded or sealed floor to contain spills, warning signs on the door, spill kit, PPE and fire extinguisher at the entrance. Liquids below powders on shelves.
  • Fertiliser: dry, on pallets off the floor, covered, stacked safely.
  • Feed and seed: dry, cool, on pallets, rodent-proof; check for mould.
  • Vaccines: in a fridge at the temperature on the label, with a thermometer and log.
  • Fuel: approved tanks, bunded, no smoking signs, extinguisher nearby.

Stock control

  • Use first-expiry, first-out (FEFO) or first-in, first-out (FIFO).
  • Record every receipt and issue in a stock register: date, product, quantity, batch, who received it and for which job.
  • Do regular stock counts and report differences.
  • Return expired or unwanted products for approved disposal.

Safety

Wear the PPE on the label when handling chemicals. Never eat, drink or smoke in the store. Clean spills immediately using the spill kit and report them.

Key points

  • Group inputs into categories and keep incompatible ones apart.
  • The label is the legal instruction: read it before storing or using.
  • Never decant chemicals into unmarked or food containers.
  • Use FIFO or FEFO and keep a stock register.
  • Chemical stores must be locked, ventilated and bunded, with a spill kit.
